title: Ignatius' cannonball
hookLine: a soldier's leg is shattered, and bored in bed he reads lives of saints

lines: NOTHING TO DO BUT LIE IN BED.
cards: A fortress wall in Pamplona, in the north of Spain, under siege. The defenders want to surrender; one young Basque nobleman talks them into fighting on.
His name is Iñigo, and he loves fine clothes, swordplay and stories of knights. Then a cannonball smashes his leg. The fortress falls, and his enemies carry him home to his family's castle at Loyola.

Surgeons set the leg badly, and it has to be broken and set again. A bone still juts out below the knee, and, by his own later account, he has it sawed off so the leg will look right in a close-fitting boot.
Then there's nothing to do but lie in bed.

teach.b: Bored, he asks for romances about knights and their ladies. The house has none. It has a life of Christ and a book of the lives of the saints, so he reads those.
And here's what he noticed, telling it later about himself in the third person, calling himself the pilgrim.

His mind kept switching between two daydreams. In one, he was a knight again, winning glory and a great lady's favor. In the other, he did what Francis and Dominic did, walking barefoot, giving everything away.
Both were pleasant while they lasted.
But afterward the knight daydream left him dry and restless, and the saint daydream left him quiet and content. He began to pay attention. Which thoughts leave you consoled?
Which leave you empty? That small noticing in a sickbed became the root of what Jesuits call discernment, and of the Spiritual Exercises he later wrote, meditations people still make on retreats.

When he could walk again, by his own account, the soldier left his sword before an image of Mary and went off as a beggar and a pilgrim. Later, with friends, he founded the Society of Jesus, the Jesuits.

Paul, in the King James Bible, hears God say: "My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness." The cannonball didn't make Ignatius holy. It made him lie still long enough to notice.
Wounded into holiness doesn't mean the wound was good. It means something good came through it.

how: Catholics honor Ignatius of Loyola as a saint and as founder of the Jesuits; people of many churches make his Spiritual Exercises on retreats, and some end each day with a short review of which moments left them consoled or empty.

games.q: you're Iñigo, stuck in bed with a shattered leg, and you ask for knightly romances. there are none. what do you do?
o: read the life of Christ and the saints, since that's all there is.
read nothing and wait it out.
send someone to town to find romances.
games.why: he reads what's there, and starts noticing that the saint daydreams leave him content while the knight daydreams leave him dry.

practice: Recall a brave person whose story you know, a saint, a grandparent, a nurse, someone from a book, and let it play for a minute. Then, as Ignatius did, notice what it leaves in you: restless or quiet, smaller or steadier.
If you pray, thank God for them; if you don't, stay with them a while.

wordCard.voice: Ignatius' cannonball. The shot that left a soldier in bed with lives of Christ and the saints, where he learned to notice which thoughts left him content.

carryVoice: Your line: wounded into holiness. Sometimes being stopped is how the noticing starts. That's day eight hundred seventy-three.
